title: Wrestling at night (Genesis 32:22–32)
hook: Jacob wrestles a stranger till dawn: I won't let you go unless you bless me

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rachel: seven years that felt like a few days, and a wedding morning with the wrong bride. Your line was love shortens the years. Whose wait did love make light? Day three hundred sixty-four.

Twenty years have passed. Jacob is rich now, with two wives, children, flocks. And he is finally going home, which means going toward Esau. Messengers come back with news: your brother is coming to meet you, with four hundred men. Jacob splits his camp in two, so that if one half is attacked the other might escape. He sends gift after gift ahead: goats, camels, cattle, donkeys. Then he sends his family across the river Jabbok in the dark. And the text says, in the King James Bible, "Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day." No name. No warning. Just a body in the dark.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS LATER.` → `ESAU AND FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `ALONE AT THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: They wrestle all night, and neither wins. Then the stranger touches Jacob's hip, and it's wrenched out of joint. Dawn is coming. The stranger says, let me go. And Jacob, limping, holding on, says the line: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The stranger asks him his name. Think about the last time Jacob was asked his name. His blind father asked, who are you, my son? And Jacob said, I am Esau. Now, holding on in the dark, he tells the truth: Jacob. And the stranger gives him a new one. "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel." And the text gives its reason: as a prince, he has had power with God and with men, and has prevailed. The man who grabbed blessings by trickery finally gets one by holding on, honestly, wounded, face to face. Who was the stranger? Genesis only says a man. Jacob names the place Peniel, face of God, because he says he saw God face to face and lived. The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. Some early Christian writers saw a glimpse of Christ in him. The text leaves it open. And Jacob walks away limping, as the sun rises. Look at this week. Sarah's grave, chesed, a bowl of stew, the goat skins, the stairway, the wrong bride, and now this river. A tangled family, and in Genesis, a promise that keeps hold of them anyway. The whole nation will carry the name given here, to a man who wouldn't let go.
screen: `NEITHER WINS. A HIP IS WRENCHED.` · `WHAT IS THY NAME? JACOB.` · `NO MORE JACOB, BUT ISRAEL.` · `PENIEL: FACE OF GOD.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT LET THEE GO, EXCEPT THOU BLESS ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wrestle honestly with one question. Settle, and breathe. Bring up a question you usually push away: about God, or suffering, or something in your own life you can't make sense of. Don't answer it. Don't tidy it. Just hold it, the way Jacob held on, and give it your real name and your real feelings. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. If you don't, simply stay with it a little longer than is comfortable. The bell holds the time.
Israel. The name given to Jacob at the river, which Genesis ties to striving with God and with men. It became the name of his whole family, and a people.
Your line: wrestle till the blessing. Today, when something hard won't resolve, don't walk away from it too soon. Stay one round longer. Day three hundred sixty-four.

screen: `DAY 364 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ESAU RUNS TO MEET HIM.`

howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Jacob's wrestling when they pray through doubt or struggle, and preachers often read it as permission to bring honest questions to God; the story is also part of the weekly Torah reading in synagogues.

notes: Meaning of 'Israel': commonly 'one who strives with God' or 'God strives'; the etymology is debated. Confirm phrasing.
'Some early Christian writers' saw Christ in the stranger (e.g. Justin Martyr's reading of theophanies). Confirm this is fair and needs no names.
